source.title: Abebe Bikila, Rome and Tokyo marathons
source.citation: 1960 Rome and 1964 Tokyo Olympic marathons; coached by Onni Niskanen

title: The marathon run barefoot
situation: An unknown Ethiopian runner arrives at the 1960 Rome Olympics and finds that the shoes he trained in have worn out. Nothing in the sponsor's kit fits him properly.
wise_response: He runs the 26 miles barefoot over Roman roads and wins, becoming the first Black African Olympic champion. Four years later, six weeks after an appendectomy, he wins again in Tokyo, this time with shoes.
why_it_worked: He had trained for years at altitude under a Swedish coach who treated him as an athlete rather than a curiosity. Equipment and circumstance set the conditions, not the ceiling.
tempting_wrong_answer: Withdraw because the equipment isn't right, or run hurt in bad shoes to protect appearances.

source.title: Wilma Rudolph, 1960 Rome Olympics
source.citation: 1960 Rome Olympics; accounts of the Rudolph family and Clarksville, Tennessee

title: The leg brace and the three golds
situation: Born premature, one of twenty-two children in segregated Tennessee, she had polio and wore a leg brace until she was nine.
wise_response: Her mother took her to a Black hospital fifty miles away twice a week for years, and her siblings took turns massaging her leg every day. She became the fastest woman in the world and won three golds in Rome.
why_it_worked: The family treated her recovery as a shared job rather than her private burden. The discipline came from being expected at practice, not from being inspired.
tempting_wrong_answer: Accept the brace as the end of the story, or leave a child to carry the work alone.

source.title: Leicester City, 2015-16 Premier League
source.citation: 2015-16 English Premier League season; Leicester City at 5,000-1 preseason odds

title: The team that was not supposed to win
situation: A newly promoted English football club, priced at 5,000-1, with a squad of players other clubs had discarded.
wise_response: The manager gave each player one job, the team defended as a unit, and the same eleven started most of the season. Nobody was asked to be a star.
why_it_worked: The system made each player's role small enough to master and important enough to keep. Cooperation beat talent because talent was not the constraint.
tempting_wrong_answer: Buy a star and build the team around him.

source.title: Yusra Mardini, Aegean crossing
source.citation: 2015 Aegean crossing; Rio 2016 Refugee Olympic Team

title: Three hours in the water
situation: A Syrian teenager fleeing the war is on a dinghy carrying twenty people when the motor dies in the Aegean Sea.
wise_response: She and her sister jump into the water and swim for three hours, pushing the boat, until everyone reaches Lesbos. A year later she swims for the refugee team at the Rio Olympics.
why_it_worked: She used the one thing she had trained for, in the moment it was needed, and did not wait for permission or a plan.
tempting_wrong_answer: Stay in the boat and hope, or save only herself.

source.title: Terry Fox, Marathon of Hope
source.citation: 1980 Marathon of Hope; Terry Fox Foundation records

title: A marathon a day on one leg
situation: A Canadian teenager loses a leg to cancer and decides to run across the country on a prosthetic leg to raise money for cancer research.
wise_response: He runs a marathon a day for 143 days, through weather and pain, until the cancer reaches his lungs. He stops, and says he will continue if he can.
why_it_worked: He asked for money for other people rather than sympathy for himself, which is why the country kept giving after he stopped.
tempting_wrong_answer: Make the story about his own survival, or quit quietly when it gets hard.

source.title: Wangari Maathai, Green Belt Movement
source.citation: Green Belt Movement, founded 1977; Nobel Peace Prize 2004

title: Trees as the argument
situation: Rural Kenyan women watch streams dry up and firewood disappear as forests are cleared. The government treats the land as a resource to be sold.
wise_response: She pays women a small wage to plant indigenous trees, village by village, and keeps planting when the government arrests her and the work is dismissed as women's business.
why_it_worked: The trees were the argument. Each surviving seedling proved the claim without a speech, and the wage made conservation a livelihood rather than a sacrifice.
tempting_wrong_answer: Petition the government and wait, or frame it as a protest that can be broken.

source.title: Nadeshiko Japan, 2011 World Cup
source.citation: 2011 FIFA Women's World Cup; four months after the Tohoku earthquake and tsunami

title: The final nobody expected
situation: Four months after the earthquake and tsunami, Japan's women's team arrives at the World Cup as underdogs, with a fraction of the resources of the favorites.
wise_response: They play a possession game built on covering for each other, come from behind twice in the final against the United States, and win on penalties.
why_it_worked: The team was organized around mutual cover rather than individual brilliance, so nobody had to win it alone.
tempting_wrong_answer: Defend desperately and hope for a lucky goal.

source.title: Nelson Mandela and the 1995 Rugby World Cup

title: The jersey he was not supposed to wear
situation: A year after apartheid, South Africa hosts the Rugby World Cup. The national team is still a symbol of white rule, and Black South Africans support whoever plays against it.
wise_response: Mandela wears the Springbok jersey and cap to the final, learns the players' names, and hands the trophy to the white captain in front of a crowd that had booed the team months earlier.
why_it_worked: He did not ask people to forget. He gave them a shared object to be proud of and let the team earn the rest.
tempting_wrong_answer: Abolish the symbol, or leave the team to its old supporters.

source.title: Nadia Comaneci, 1976 Montreal
source.citation: 1976 Montreal Olympics; coached by Bela and Marta Karolyi

title: The scoreboard that could not show ten
situation: A fourteen-year-old Romanian gymnast competes in a sport dominated by older Soviet athletes, on equipment that has never produced a perfect score.
wise_response: She performs a routine so precise that the scoreboard cannot display 10.0 and shows 1.00. She does it six more times at the same Games.
why_it_worked: Her coach had drilled the routine until the performance did not depend on the occasion, and she competed as if the crowd were not there.
tempting_wrong_answer: Play safe to protect a medal, or perform for the judges.

source.title: Milkha Singh, 1960 Rome 400m
source.citation: 1960 Rome Olympics; later Asian and Commonwealth Games

title: Fourth by a fraction
situation: An Indian runner orphaned in the Partition violence runs the 400m final in Rome, leads until the last stretch, and finishes fourth, missing a medal by a fraction.
wise_response: He does not dispute the result or blame the lane. He goes home, trains, wins gold at the Asian and Commonwealth Games, and spends decades coaching young Indian athletes.
why_it_worked: He treated the loss as information rather than an identity, and turned the near-miss into a standard for the people who came after him.
tempting_wrong_answer: Replay the race in his head, or retire while the story is still about the injustice.
